questions.q: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of the conservation of:
questions.solution:
$\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$ — heat supplied to a system either raises its internal energy or is spent as work done by it.

It is simply the conservation of **energy** extended to include heat as a form of energy transfer.

An adiabatic process is one with **no heat exchange**: $\Delta Q = 0$.

The first law then gives $\Delta W = -\Delta U$ — any work done by the gas comes entirely out of its internal energy, so an adiabatic expansion cools the gas.

$\Delta U = 0$ and $\Delta T = 0$ describe an **isothermal** process instead.

questions.q: The rms speed of gas molecules is proportional to:
questions.solution:
$v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$, so $v_{rms} \propto \mathbf{\sqrt{T}}$ at fixed molar mass.

Quadrupling the absolute temperature only doubles the rms speed. Note also $v_{rms} \propto 1/\sqrt{M}$, which is why hydrogen leaks away from a planet's atmosphere and nitrogen does not.

questions.q: For a monatomic ideal gas, the ratio $\gamma = C_p/C_v$ is:
questions.solution:
A monatomic gas has $f = 3$ degrees of freedom, so $C_v = \tfrac{3}{2}R$ and $C_p = \tfrac{5}{2}R$.

$\gamma = \dfrac{5/2}{3/2} = \dfrac{5}{3} \approx \mathbf{1.67}$.

The general rule is $\gamma = 1 + 2/f$: a diatomic gas ($f = 5$) gives $1.4$ and a polyatomic one ($f = 6$) gives $1.33$.

questions.q: The efficiency of a Carnot engine working between temperatures $T_1$ (source) and $T_2$ (sink) is:
questions.solution:
$\eta = \mathbf{1 - \dfrac{T_2}{T_1}}$, with both temperatures in **kelvin**.

It is the maximum efficiency any engine can have between those two reservoirs, and reaching $100\%$ would need a sink at absolute zero.

questions.q: In any spontaneous process in an isolated system, the entropy:
questions.solution:
The second law says $\Delta S \ge 0$ for an isolated system: entropy **increases** for an irreversible process and stays constant for a reversible one.

This is the law that gives time a direction — it is why heat flows from hot to cold and never the other way by itself.

questions.q: For an adiabatic process in an ideal gas, which relation holds?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}}$, with the equivalent forms $TV^{\gamma-1} = $ constant and $P^{1-\gamma}T^{\gamma} = $ constant.

$PV = $ constant is the **isothermal** case. Since $\gamma > 1$, an adiabatic curve on a $P$–$V$ diagram is always steeper than the isothermal one through the same point.

questions.q: The average kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas depends only on:
questions.solution:
By the equipartition theorem, the mean translational kinetic energy is

$\bar{K} = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$

It depends **only on the absolute temperature** — not on the mass of the molecule, nor on the pressure or volume.

So at the same temperature a hydrogen molecule and an oxygen molecule have the same average kinetic energy; the lighter one simply moves faster.

questions.q: In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas:
questions.solution:
For an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on temperature, so an isothermal process has $\Delta U = 0$.

The first law then reduces to

$\Delta Q = \Delta W$

— every joule of heat absorbed comes straight back out as work done by the gas.

questions.q: A Carnot engine works between $500\ \text{K}$ and $300\ \text{K}$. Find its efficiency as a percentage.
A gas absorbs $200\ \text{J}$ of heat and does $80\ \text{J}$ of work. Find the increase in its internal energy, in joules.
The rms speed of a gas at $300\ \text{K}$ is $v$. At what temperature, in kelvin, is the rms speed $2v$?
For a diatomic gas (rigid, $f = 5$), find $C_v$ as a multiple of $R$. Give the multiple.
questions.solution:
$C_v = \dfrac{f}{2}R = \dfrac{5}{2}R = \mathbf{2.5}\,R$.

And $C_p = C_v + R = 3.5R$, giving $\gamma = 3.5/2.5 = 1.4$ as expected.

questions.q: A monatomic gas ($\gamma = 5/3$) at volume $V$ is compressed adiabatically to $V/8$. By what factor does the temperature rise?
questions.solution:
For an adiabatic process, $TV^{\gamma-1} = $ constant, and $\gamma - 1 = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \left(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{\gamma-1} = 8^{2/3}$

$8^{1/3} = 2$, so $8^{2/3} = 2^{2} = \mathbf{4}$.

The temperature becomes four times as large — this is why a bicycle pump warms up.

questions.q: Using the kinetic theory of gases, derive the expression $P = \tfrac{1}{3}\rho v_{rms}^{2}$ for the pressure of an ideal gas. Hence show that the mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is $\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$.
questions.solution:
**The assumptions.** The gas consists of $N$ identical molecules of mass $m$ in a cube of side $L$, moving randomly, of negligible size compared with their separation, colliding elastically with the walls and with each other, and exerting no forces between collisions.

**One molecule, one wall.** Take a molecule with $x$-component of velocity $v_x$ hitting the wall perpendicular to the $x$-axis. The collision is elastic, so the velocity component reverses and the momentum change is

$\Delta p = -mv_x - (mv_x) = -2mv_x$

The momentum given to the wall is $2mv_x$.

**How often.** The molecule travels $2L$ between successive impacts on that same wall, so the time between them is

$\Delta t = \dfrac{2L}{v_x}$

**Force from one molecule.**

$F = \dfrac{2mv_x}{2L/v_x} = \dfrac{mv_x^{2}}{L}$

**All the molecules.** Summing over all $N$ molecules:

$F_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{m}{L}\sum v_x^{2} = \dfrac{mN\overline{v_x^{2}}}{L}$

**Isotropy.** The motion is random, so no direction is special:

$\overline{v_x^{2}} = \overline{v_y^{2}} = \overline{v_z^{2}} = \tfrac{1}{3}\overline{v^{2}}$

Hence $F_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{mN\overline{v^{2}}}{3L}$.

**Pressure** is force per unit area, and the wall has area $L^{2}$:

$P = \dfrac{F}{L^{2}} = \dfrac{mN\overline{v^{2}}}{3L^{3}} = \dfrac{mN\overline{v^{2}}}{3V}$

Since the density is $\rho = mN/V$:

$\boxed{P = \tfrac{1}{3}\rho\,v_{rms}^{2}}$

where $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\overline{v^{2}}}$.

**Connecting to temperature.** Rewrite as $PV = \tfrac{1}{3}Nm\,v_{rms}^{2}$ and compare with the ideal gas equation $PV = Nk_BT$:

$\tfrac{1}{3}Nm\,v_{rms}^{2} = Nk_BT$

$m\,v_{rms}^{2} = 3k_BT$

The mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is therefore

$\bar{K} = \tfrac{1}{2}m\,v_{rms}^{2} = \boxed{\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT}$

**What this means.** Temperature is **not** a separate quantity that happens to correlate with molecular motion — it **is** a measure of the mean kinetic energy per molecule. The result also explains why $\bar{K}$ is independent of the molecular mass: at a given temperature, heavier molecules simply move more slowly.
